preamble: Loss of pharyngealization with affrication: the emphatic sibilant [sˤ] becomes the plain affricate [ts]. In Hebrew, ṣādē (from Proto-Semitic *ṣ, reconstructed as *tsʼ, and from *ṣ́ and *ṯ̣, which merged with it) is [sˤ] in Wiktionary's Biblical Hebrew forms and in the Tiberian and Yemenite traditions, but [ts] in Ashkenazi and Israeli Hebrew; Wikipedia describes Biblical/Mishnaic sˤ as "de-pharyngealized and affricated" to Israeli t͡s. Wikipedia attributes the loss of the emphatics in Ashkenazi and non-Oriental Israeli Hebrew to the influence of European languages. Steiner (1982) and Kogan (2011: 62–63) argue instead that the affricate is old, which would make Hebrew a direct *tsʼ > ts; the atlas follows the two-step account. Sephardi readings vary between [s], [ts] and [sˤ] (צדק /ˈse.dek/, צל West /ˈt͡sel/, East /ˈsˤel/).

examples.note: The initial ʕ is lost as well.

sources: Steiner, R. C. (1982). Affricated Ṣade in the Semitic Languages. American Academy for Jewish Research.
Kogan, L. (2011). Proto-Semitic Phonetics and Phonology. In S. Weninger (Ed.), The Semitic Languages: An International Handbook, 54–151. De Gruyter.
